lessons.title: Measuring Returns Fairly: CAGR vs IRR vs Distribution Yield

children.text: In one week, Pooja, a finance manager in Mumbai, hears three return claims. Her mutual fund app says her Nifty index fund has a 5-year CAGR of 14%. A PE fund manager says his last fund delivered a 24% IRR. A relative says his Andheri flat "gives 9% yield." Pooja's instinct is to rank them: 24% beats 14% beats 9%. That instinct is wrong, because the three numbers measure three different things. Chapter 4 profiled each alternative on its own. Chapter 5 puts them on the same scale, and it starts here, with the three ways returns are quoted and the tricks each one allows.

body.text: CAGR measures how fast a lump sum grew. IRR measures the return on money that went in and came out at different times. Yield measures only the income. Compare any two of them directly and you are comparing distance with speed with fuel efficiency.

body.caption: The three return measures at a glance

cells: At what steady yearly rate did a single investment grow?
Lump sums, index and fund performance, property bought and sold once
Money added or withdrawn along the way
What yearly return makes all my cash flows, in and out, worth zero today?
SIPs, PE and VC funds, capital calls, rental property with ongoing cash flows

How much income does it pay each year, relative to a price?
Comparing income from REITs, InvITs, bonds and rented property

children.text: CAGR: The Speed of a Lump Sum

You have used CAGR throughout this course. It is the cleanest measure when one amount goes in at the start and one amount comes out at the end. Mutual fund factsheets quote it because it strips out the effect of when individual investors added or removed money, so it measures the fund manager, not the investors.

body.text: Beware of short periods presented as annual rates. A 15% gain in four months becomes an "annualised" return of over 50%, which no one should expect to repeat. Unless an investment has run for at least a year, and preferably a full cycle, ask for the actual return, not the annualised one.

children.text: IRR and XIRR: Returns When Money Moves In and Out

markDefs.definition: Internal rate of return: the single annual discount rate at which the present value of all money invested equals the present value of all money received.
The spreadsheet version of IRR that uses actual transaction dates, so it works for irregular cash flows such as SIPs, capital calls and distributions.

children.text: When money goes in and comes out at different times, CAGR breaks down. The
IRR
handles this by finding the one rate that balances every outflow against every inflow. For real-life dates, use
XIRR
in Excel or Google Sheets. It is the figure your mutual fund statement shows for your own SIP returns.

body.caption: CF = cash flow in year t, negative when you invest, positive when you receive money

children.text: IRR is the right tool for PE funds, SIPs and property with rent. It also has three weaknesses that fund managers know very well.
Weakness 1: IRR ignores how much wealth you actually made

markDefs.definition: Total money received divided by total money invested. A 2x multiple means you got back twice what you put in, regardless of how long it took.

children.text: A high IRR can come from a small gain earned quickly. Always read it next to the
money multiple

cells: Value after 8 years if Fund A's ₹130 is reinvested at 7%
Value after 8 years if Fund A's ₹130 is reinvested at 12%

children.text: Fund A's 30% IRR only beats Fund B if you can reinvest the proceeds at a strong rate for the next seven years. The IRR alone cannot tell you that. A manager quoting a high IRR without the multiple may be showing you speed without distance.
Weakness 2: Timing tricks can lift IRR without making you richer

body.title: Show me how a borrowing line raises a fund's IRR

markDefs.definition: A short-term loan a fund uses to make investments before calling money from its investors. It delays capital calls, which shortens the period the IRR is measured over.

children.text: Many funds use a
subscription line

: they borrow to buy an investment first and call investors' money later. The investor's money is then "at work" for a shorter time, which raises the IRR, even though the interest on the borrowing reduces what the investor actually receives.

content.caption: Same deal, with and without a one-year borrowing line (₹, illustrative)

children.text: The IRR went up while the investor's multiple went down. If the fund's carry or marketing is based on IRR, the manager benefits. Always ask whether a fund's reported IRR uses a borrowing line.
Weakness 3: A fund IRR and an index CAGR are not the same kind of number

markDefs.definition: Public market equivalent: a method that invests a private fund's exact cash flows into a public index, on the same dates, to see whether the fund beat what the index would have delivered.

children.text: A fund's IRR is money-weighted and the Nifty's CAGR is time-weighted, so putting them side by side is unfair in both directions. The fair test is a
public market equivalent (PME)
: pretend every capital call went into a Nifty index fund instead, and every distribution came out of it. If the index version ends up with more money, the fund did not earn its fees and lock-in.

body.latex: \text{PME ratio} = \frac{\text{Distributions grown at the index return to the end date}}{\text{Capital calls grown at the index return to the end date}}
body.caption: Above 1: the fund beat the index. Below 1: the index would have done better.
A PE fund vs the same cash flows in a Nifty fund earning 12% a year (₹ lakh, illustrative)

children.text: A 1.8x multiple sounds like a success. But the PME ratio of 0.95 says the same money, invested in and taken out of the Nifty on the same dates, would have ended up about 5% richer, with daily liquidity throughout.

columns.label: Time-weighted (CAGR on a factsheet)
points: Measures the investment, not the investor
Ignores when money was added or withdrawn
Used for mutual fund and index performance
Fair for comparing managers who do not control cash flows

columns.label: Money-weighted (IRR or XIRR)
points: Rewards or penalises the timing of cash flows
Used for SIP statements, PE and VC funds, property with rent
Fair when the manager controls when money goes in and out

children.text: Yield: Income Only, and on Which Price?

markDefs.definition: Annual income divided by the price you originally paid. It grows as income rises, but says nothing about what your money could earn if invested elsewhere today.
Annual income divided by the asset's current market value. This is the yield that matters for deciding whether to keep holding it.

children.text: Yield only counts income, so it misses price changes entirely, and as Chapter 4 showed with InvITs, it can include your own capital coming back. It can also be calculated on two different prices. Pooja's relative bought his Andheri flat for ₹40 lakh years ago and now rents it for ₹30,000 a month, or ₹3.6 lakh a year. That is a 9%
yield on cost
. But the flat is now worth about ₹1.4 crore, so its
current yield
is only about 2.6%. If he sold and bought a G-Sec, his income would more than double.

body.title: Yield on cost vs current yield
body.prompt: A flat in Chennai was bought for ₹25 lakh in 2008. It now rents for ₹25,000 a month and is worth about ₹90 lakh. What is its current yield, in percent, before costs? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Annual rent is ₹25,000 × 12 = ₹3 lakh. Current yield is ₹3 lakh ÷ ₹90 lakh ≈ 3.3%. On the original ₹25 lakh, the yield on cost is 12%, which sounds excellent but is irrelevant to the decision of whether to keep ₹90 lakh tied up earning 3.3% before costs.

children.text: Same Money Multiple, Very Different Returns

body.title: Annual return from doubling your money, by how long it takes (%)

children.text: "We doubled investors' money" can mean a strong 14.9% a year or a below-FD 5.9% a year. A multiple without a time period is as incomplete as an IRR without a multiple.

body.title: Rank the claims
body.question: Pooja hears: an index fund with a 14% 5-year CAGR, a PE fund with a 24% IRR, and a flat with a 9% yield on its purchase price. What is the most sensible first step before ranking them?
options: Rank them by the headline number: 24%, then 14%, then 9%
Convert them to comparable measures: get the PE fund's multiple and PME, and the flat's current yield and total return
Pick the flat, because yield is the most reliable number
Ignore all three, because returns cannot be compared across assets
body.explanation: Each number measures something different. The PE IRR needs its multiple and a PME check against the index. The flat's 9% is yield on cost, not current yield or total return. Only after converting can the three be compared fairly.

body.title: The spreadsheet function
body.textWithBlank: To calculate the return on irregular cash flows with actual dates, such as SIP instalments or capital calls, you use the ___ function in Excel or Google Sheets.
body.explanation: XIRR takes a list of cash flows and their dates and returns the annualised money-weighted return. Enter money invested as negative numbers and money received, including the current value, as positive numbers.

body.title: The 24% IRR pitch
body.scenario: A PE fund manager meets Pooja and says: "Fund II has delivered a 24% net IRR in its first three years, versus the Nifty's 14% CAGR over the same period. That is 10 points of outperformance a year." The fund is eight years from the end of its life. Most of its value is in unrealised holdings, and it uses a subscription line.
body.prompt: What questions should Pooja ask, and why is the comparison with the Nifty misleading?
body.modelAnswer:
Questions to ask:
1. What is the money multiple, and how much of it is actual cash distributed versus estimated value? A 24% IRR over three years could be a modest multiple, mostly on paper.
2. Does the IRR use a subscription line? If so, what is the IRR from the date investors' money would have been called without it?
3. How are unrealised holdings valued, and by whom? Early IRRs rest heavily on appraisals.
4. What is the PME ratio against the Nifty using the fund's actual cash flow dates?
5. How did Fund I's IRR and multiple look at year 3 compared with its final result?

Why the comparison misleads:
- The fund's IRR is money-weighted and based on its own cash flow timing; the Nifty's CAGR is time-weighted. They are different kinds of numbers.
- Three years is early in an 8 to 10-year fund. Early IRRs can be inflated by subscription lines and optimistic marks, and they often fall later.
- The Nifty figure is realised, liquid and verifiable. Most of the fund's figure is not.

The fair comparison is a PME using the same cash flows, ideally at the end of the fund's life, alongside the multiple of cash actually returned.

cards.definition: The steady annual growth rate of a single lump sum from start to end.
The annual rate that makes the present value of all cash flows in and out equal zero.
IRR calculated with actual transaction dates, used for SIPs and irregular cash flows.
Total received divided by total invested, ignoring time.
A fund's short-term borrowing that delays capital calls and can raise reported IRR.
Public market equivalent: tests a fund against an index using the fund's own cash flow dates.

cards.term: Yield on cost vs current yield
cards.definition: Income divided by the original price vs income divided by today's value. Only current yield guides a hold-or-sell decision.

points: CAGR, IRR and yield measure different things: lump-sum growth, return on moving cash flows, and income only.
Never compare a fund's IRR directly with an index CAGR; use a PME, which runs the fund's cash flows through the index on the same dates.
Always read IRR next to the money multiple: 30% for 1.3x in one year can leave you poorer than 12.1% for 2.5x over eight years.
Subscription lines can raise IRR while lowering the multiple, as in the example where IRR rose from 14.9% to 16.7% and the multiple fell from 2.0x to 1.85x.
Doubling money is 14.9% a year over 5 years but only 5.9% a year over 12, so always ask how long.
Use current yield, not yield on cost, when deciding whether an income asset still deserves your money.
